Empirical Research Plan – “Class Size and Student Achievement”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Chosen method: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (fuzzy-RDD) interpreted as a two‐stage least squares (IV) model.

Why appropriate?  
• U.S. public elementary and secondary schools typically face hard or soft maximum-class-size “caps” set by state statute, district collective-bargaining agreements, or fire-code/room-capacity rules (e.g., 30 in grades 4-6, 25 in K-3 in many states).  
• Because the number of pupils in a given grade at a school is determined by local birth-cohort fluctuations and in- and out-migration—forces plausibly exogenous to the school—enrollment occasionally crosses these caps.  
• When enrollment crosses a cap, the school must open an additional classroom, producing an exogenous, discontinuous drop in average class size (first stage). Student achievement is smooth in enrollment in the absence of such a rule, so any jump in outcomes at the cap can be attributed causally to the class-size change.  
• Because the cap is binding only for the part of the distribution above the cutoff, treatment assignment is “imperfect”—hence, a fuzzy rather than sharp RD, estimated with 2SLS.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Running variable (R): Grade-level enrollment at school s in grade g and year t (N_sgt).  
Cutoffs (c): Known maximum-class-size caps, typically c = 25, 30, 35. We pool all multiples of c (k·c, k = 1, 2, 3…).  

Treatment variable (T): Realized average class size in grade g, school s, year t (CS_sgt). Lower CS (smaller classes) is “treated.”  

• Treated observations: Units just above the cap where an additional class is opened, reducing CS_sgt.  
• Control observations: Units just below the cap where only one (or k) class(es) are formed, yielding larger CS_sgt.  
• Timing: The “event” is contemporaneous; measurement is within the same academic year.

First-stage (Z): A dummy 1{R_sgt > c_k} that equals one when enrollment is above the nearest cap threshold and zero otherwise.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Continuity of Potential Outcomes: In the absence of the cap rule, expected achievement would vary smoothly with enrollment at the cutoff.  
Plausibility: Cohort size shocks come from demographic drift, not educational policy. No reason for a discrete jump exactly at c absent the rule.

A2. No Precise Manipulation of Running Variable: Schools, parents, or administrators cannot finely manipulate N_sgt to land just below the cap (e.g., by holding students back).  
Plausibility: Enrollment is measured on fall census day; individual parents cannot easily coordinate; we will test with McCrary density plots.

A3. First-Stage Relevance (Monotonicity): Crossing the cap always (weakly) lowers average class size; no schools “defy” the rule by keeping class size constant.  
Plausibility: Compliance is enforced by district staffing formulas; we can verify empirically.

A4. Exclusion Restriction: Crossing the cap affects achievement only through its impact on class size, not through simultaneous, discontinuous changes in other resources (e.g., aides, materials).  
Plausibility: Budgets and other inputs are set per-pupil and adjust smoothly; we will test for discontinuities in observable resources.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & REMEDIES  

T1. Manipulation/Sorting at Cutoff.  
  – Test: McCrary density test; examine distribution of enrollment.  
  – Remedy: If manipulation detected, apply “donut RD” (drop ±1 pupil) or use larger bandwidth selection models.

T2. Other Inputs Jump at Threshold.  
  – Test: RD on staffing FTE, per-pupil spending, teacher experience.  
  – Remedy: Control for any input that shows a discontinuity; interpret as “reduced-form” if exclusion fails.

T3. Heterogeneous Caps & Measurement Error.  
  – Solution: Collect state/district-specific cap values; allow for heterogeneity by interacting cutoff indicators with state dummies; use multiple thresholds with cluster-robust SEs. Validate class-size drop magnitudes.

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE (executable)

```r
# --- 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data manipulation
library(fixest)       # fast OLS / IV with fixed effects
library(rdrobust)     # canonical RD
library(ggplot2)      # plots

# --- 1. Load Data -----------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("us_class_size_panel.csv")   # one row per student-year

# --- 2. Variable Construction ----------------------------------------------
# school-grade-year cell
dt[, sgty_id := .GRP, by = .(school_id, grade, year)]

# aggregate to cell level for RD
cell <- dt[, .(
  enroll     = .N,
  mean_score = mean(achievement_score),
  class_size = unique(class_size)        # assume avg reported
), by = .(school_id, grade, year)]

# identify cap (can vary by state/grade; assume provided)
# Example: cap_elt = 25 ; cap_ms = 30
cell[, cap := fifelse(grade <= 3, 25L, 30L)]

# distance from nearest lower multiple of cap
cell[, running := enroll %% cap]         # remainder
cell[, threshold := enroll - running]    # lower multiple
cell[, above_cut := (running == 0) & (enroll > 0)]  # exact multiples
cell[, treat_z := as.integer(running == 0 & enroll > 0)] # fuzzy instrument

# keep bandwidth +/-10 around each multiple of cap
cell[, dist := enroll - threshold - cap]   # centered at cap
band <- 10
rd_sample <- cell[abs(dist) <= band]

# --- 3. Main Fuzzy RD (2SLS) ----------------------------------------------
# first stage: does crossing cap reduce class size?
fs <- feols(class_size ~ treat_z | enroll + threshold, data = rd_sample)
summary(fs)

# second stage / 2SLS for outcome
iv_mod <- feols(mean_score ~ 1 | treat_z ~ class_size | enroll + threshold,
                data = rd_sample, vcov = "cluster:school_id")
summary(iv_mod)

# rdrobust implementation (bandwidth selected automatically)
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = rd_sample$mean_score,
                   x = rd_sample$dist,
                   c = 0,
                   fuzzy = rd_sample$class_size)
summary(rd_out)

# --- 4. Robustness: Different Bandwidths & Donut ---------------------------
for(bw in c(5, 7, 12)) {
  tmp <- rd_sample[abs(dist) <= bw]
  mod <- feols(mean_score ~ 1 | treat_z ~ class_size | enroll + threshold,
               data = tmp, vcov = "cluster:school_id")
  print(paste("Bandwidth", bw))
  print(coeftable(mod))
}

# McCrary density test
dens <- rddensity(cell$enroll, c = cell$cap)
summary(dens)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Economic theory (education production functions and Tennessee STAR findings) predicts that smaller classes raise achievement, especially in early grades. I expect:  
• Direction: Negative first stage (class size falls at cutoff).  
• Reduced-form jump: Positive (scores rise).  
• Local Average Treatment Effect (early grades): ≈ 0.05–0.10 SD increase in test scores for a 5‐pupil reduction (≈ 0.01–0.02 SD per pupil).

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (fuzzy-RDD)  
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)

C1 Running-variable manipulation test passed (McCrary) ………… 1  
C2 Covariate balance at cutoff (demographics smooth) ……………… 1  
C3 Strong, monotone first stage (CS drops at cap) …………………… 1  
C4 No other discontinuities in resources at cap …………………… 0.5  
C5 Robustness to bandwidth/functional form ………………………… 1  

Overall score: 4.5 / 5 – credible but still vigilant about simultaneous resource changes.
